title: Intrinsic spin-orbit coupling in graphene stacks
authors: Guillermo Parra-Martinez, Alejandro Jimeno-Pozo, Ady Stern, Jose Angel Silva-Guillén, Francisco Guinea
abstract: The effect of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in monolayer graphene has been thoroughly studied in the past. Its impact is commonly disregarded since the electronic structure of graphene is almost unaffected. Consequently, SOC has also been ignored in other graphitic systems. In this work, we calculate the intrinsic SOC in stacks of graphene layers from a model that includes all the valence orbitals of carbon as well as the intra-atomic SOC.The leading spin-orbit term in a graphene multilayer combines a Rashba-like spin-flip process with interlayer hopping. We find that this intrinsic term modifies the phase diagram and Fermi surfaces of finite rhombohedral stacks, and it leads to a distinct density-dependence of the magnetization in weak magnetic fields. This Letter shows that, unlike in the single-layer case, SOC has important consequences in multilayer graphitic systems and it should not be neglected when studying their physical properties.
summary: This work calculates the intrinsic spin-orbit coupling in stacked graphene layers, demonstrating that this effect is crucial and cannot be ignored as in single-layer graphene. By analyzing the resulting Hamiltonian using mean-field theory, the authors map out new correlated phases and propose experimental diagnostics based on magnetization to confirm the importance of interlayer SOC.
main_problem: To determine the physical consequences of intrinsic spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in multilayer graphene stacks, arguing that SOC effects are significant in these systems, unlike the single-layer case.
main_result: The intrinsic SOC term ($\lambda_4$) is the dominant effect in multilayer graphene, modifying the phase diagram and leading to a distinct, measurable density-dependence of magnetization in weak magnetic fields.
method: The study employs tight-binding models, mean-field Hartree-Fock theory, and continuum approximations to analyze the effective low-energy Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The system is graphene stacks, specifically rhombohedral multilayer graphene (RMG) and $	ext{R}4	ext{G}$. The analysis incorporates the atomic SOC and derives an effective Hamiltonian containing terms like the Kane-Mele term ($\lambda_1$) and the crucial interlayer spin-flip term ($\lambda_4$).
key_observables: Phase diagrams, Fermi surface topologies (quantified by Euler characteristic $\chi_\xi$ and index $\Lambda$), and the density-dependence of magnetization ($\langle s_z angle$).
important_parameters: SOC strengths ($\lambda_1$ vs. $\lambda_4$), carrier density ($n$), and external magnetic field strength ($B$).
main_assumptions: The analysis uses a continuum model and neglects effects due to a possible displacement field.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the derivation of SOC terms, phase diagrams showing transitions between correlated metallic states, and the topology of the Fermi surface in different regimes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the necessity of including intrinsic SOC in multilayer systems, deriving the effective low-energy Hamiltonian, applying Hartree-Fock theory to map out the phase diagram, and finally using magnetization diagnostics to distinguish between different SOC mechanisms.
why_interesting: The detailed analysis of spin-valley locking and the emergence of correlated phases due to SOC provides rich theoretical models relevant to topological quantum materials and strongly interacting electron systems.
